newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Samuel Jackson - A kinder, gentler action hero?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Samuel Jackson - A kinder, gentler action hero?.

text.p: In "Pulp Fiction," Samuel Jackson won rave reviews as a hitman with a conscience.
It may have seemed like something only an offbeat director like Quentin Tarantino could have dreamed up, but for Jackson it was just the kind of character he could relate to.

In fact, Jackson told Reuters, characters like Jules, the sensitive criminal, are the ones he most enjoys because of the way they upset stereotypes. But bringing a personal touch to his work gets difficult when he plays action heroes, who are not supposed to reveal anything more than a tough exterior.

His new film, "The Long Kiss Goodnight," is packed with shootings, dramatic chase scenes and escapes that defy logic -- the sort of stuff that does not leave much room for things like character development. But to hear Jackson's description, you would never know the detective he plays in the film is working with a former secret agent to derail a massive terrorist conspiracy.

"There are a lot of people like Mitch in this world," Jackson said of his character, "people who don't have a lot of self-confidence, who have been damaged by their experiences to the point that they think they are not worthy."

How does he squeeze all this psychoanalysis into a film where the pitch of action is so intense that characters barely pause long enough to have a conversation? With blood, he says. And tears. Although he survives multiple gunshots, powerful explosions and a jump from a tall building into a frozen lake, he does so with less bravado than the typical action hero.

The fear in his eyes, the quiver in his limbs and the dried blood that covers his face in the final scene, he says, differentiate him from the other bullet-dodging, flame-resistant heroes that grace the big screen.
"I actually think you can watch Geena (co-star Geena Davis) and me get into trouble and think sometimes, well maybe we're not going to make it," he said.
While bringing this sort of realism to a highly unrealistic story is a personal triumph for Jackson, he concedes it is not the model for professional success.

"A lot of times you watch movies like this and the people whose names are above the title, say Arnold or Bruce, when they're in jeopardy, they're not really in jeopardy at all," he said of box office sensations Arnold Schwarzenegger and Bruce Willis. "You know they are going to escape in some spectacular way."

Jackson calls those kinds of figures "Clint Eastwoodesque, steel-jowled, look-death-in-the-face-and-not-react-to-it kind of guys who dispatch people with as much emotion as they would stomp on an ant hill."

His own resistance to that proven format probably stems from his versatile resume. On screen, he has done comedy as well as serious drama and action. He also spent more than a decade in theatre with the Negro Ensemble Company and other groups. Today Jackson is one of only a few actors sought after for both small "art films" and action-packed blockbusters.

Yet he is quick to defend what he says is Hollywood's favourite film format, the kind full of special effects and big-name stars, "where they don't spend a lot of time worrying about plot line or anything else." After all, he says, those are the only films that consistently make money.
He said he would like to see the young people who flock to action films go see "Trainspotting," the controversial Scottish film about a group of heroin junkies.

"But they're not going to because somebody has already put another label on it, the 'art movie,'" he said, making quotation marks with his fingers. "Once you call it an art movie it doesn't matter how good it is. A certain segment of the population is not going to see it because there's nothing blowing up and nobody getting shot."
